sources.citation: Magaziner J, Hawkes W, Hebel JR, Zimmerman SI, Fox KM, Dolan M, et al. Recovery from hip fracture in eight areas of function. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2000;55(9):M498-507.
sources.design: Prospective multicentre cohort, 2-year follow-up

sources.citation: Dyer SM, Crotty M, Fairhall N, Magaziner J, Beaupre LA, Cameron ID, et al. A critical review of the long-term disability outcomes following hip fracture. BMC Geriatr. 2016;16(1):158.

sources.quality_note: Highest-level evidence; moderate certainty for the inpatient 'poor outcome' composite; heterogeneous interventions; home-based supported discharge evidence very low certainty.

sources.citation: Harrison JK, Garrido AG, Rhynas SJ, Logan G, MacLullich AM, MacArthur J, et al. New institutionalisation following acute hospital admission: a retrospective cohort study. Age Ageing. 2017;46(2):238-244.

sources.citation: Scottish Government. Choosing a care home on discharge from hospital: guidance. Edinburgh: Scottish Government [web page not opened].
sources.design: Government guidance (not opened)
sources.population_setting: Scotland, adults in hospital needing a care home place
sources.tool_used: WebSearch (official page could not be opened; also listed: publications.scot.nhs.uk/files/cel2013-32.pdf)
sources.correction_check: Not applicable (policy document); current version and wording not verified.
sources.quality_note: Search-engine summary only, not verbatim page text. Not sufficient for an essential claim; do not quote or paraphrase it as the guidance's wording.

sources.citation: Loggers SAI, Willems HC, Van Balen R, Gosens T, Polinder S, Ponsen KJ, et al. Evaluation of quality of life after nonoperative or operative management of proximal femoral fractures in frail institutionalized patients: the FRAIL-HIP study. JAMA Surg. 2022;157(5):424-434.
sources.design: Prospective multicentre cohort; treatment chosen through shared decision-making (not randomised); non-inferiority comparison of proxy-rated quality of life

sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (abstract); Scite search_literature full-text excerpts (PMC full text not returned by PubMed tool)
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. PubMed author search for published errata/retractions (Ottesen, Kammerlander, Loggers): none linked to this article. The three Osteoporos Int corrections (PMIDs 36648543, 40387895, 40764419) concern the separate FRAIL-HIP cost-utility paper, not this article.
sources.quality_note: Only sizeable prospective study of this choice; selection by choice means mortality differences reflect who chose, not the effect of not operating (authors say so). Quality of life proxy-rated. Abstract week-1 confidence intervals look internally inconsistent (0.26 [0.11-0.23]); do not quote EQ-5D figures.

sources.citation: Kammerlander C, Pfeufer D, Lisitano LA, Mehaffey S, Böcker W, Neuerburg C. Inability of older adult patients with hip fracture to maintain postoperative weight-bearing restrictions. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2018;100(11):936-941.

sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. PubMed author search for published errata/retractions (Ottesen, Kammerlander, Loggers): none linked to this article.
sources.quality_note: Very small, single centre, one gait session after physiotherapy training; abstract's control-group figures are reported two ways (14 of 18 and 16 of 18).

sources.citation: Pfeufer D, Zeller A, Mehaffey S, Böcker W, Kammerlander C, Neuerburg C. Weight-bearing restrictions reduce postoperative mobility in elderly hip fracture patients. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg. 2019;139(9):1253-1259.

sources.quality_note: Small, non-randomised (pre-post); same research group as Kammerlander 2018.

sources.citation: Ottesen TD, McLynn RP, Galivanche AR, Bagi PS, Zogg CK, Rubin LE, et al. Increased complications in geriatric patients with a fracture of the hip whose postoperative weight-bearing is restricted: an analysis of 4918 patients. Bone Joint J. 2018;100-B(10):1377-1384.

sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. PubMed author search for published errata/retractions (Ottesen, Kammerlander, Loggers): none linked to this article.
sources.quality_note: Observational; confounding by indication likely (restriction is prescribed for harder fractures and fixations). Abstract arithmetic inconsistent: 3668 is given as 63.53% of 4918, but 3668/4918 is about 75%; do not quote the percentage.

sources.citation: Tarrant SM, Attia J, Balogh ZJ. The influence of weight-bearing status on post-operative mobility and outcomes in geriatric hip fracture. Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg. 2022;48(5):4093-4103.
sources.design: Prospective observational cohort with adjusted and mediation analyses

sources.quality_note: Conflicting evidence for the harm claim: only 58 had restricted weight-bearing, so estimates are imprecise.

sources.citation: Xu S, Gao F, Chen Y, Liu G, Peng K, Zhang J, et al. Impact of postoperative weight-bearing protocols on prognosis in geriatric hip fracture patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Clin Med. 2026;15(10):3912.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO-registered), 10 studies (1 RCT, 9 cohorts), GRADE
sources.population_setting: 5806 patients aged 65 and over after hip fracture surgery, unrestricted versus restricted weight-bearing
sources.quality_note: Most recent synthesis; low to very low certainty; abstract has garbled symbols and an implausible absolute risk difference (-0.10%), so quote only the direction and certainty.

sources.citation: Taraldsen K, Sletvold O, Thingstad P, Saltvedt I, Granat MH, Lydersen S, et al. Physical behavior and function early after hip fracture surgery in patients receiving comprehensive geriatric care or orthopedic care: a randomized controlled trial. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2014;69(3):338-45.
sources.design: Randomised controlled trial (part of the Trondheim Hip Fracture Trial)
sources.population_setting: 397 home-dwelling people aged 70 and over with hip fracture who could walk 10 m before; Trondheim, Norway; 317 wore a body-worn monitor for 24 hours on day 4 after surgery
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata (full text closed; Scite gave no excerpts)
sources.correction_check: Scite editorialNotices checked 2026-09-25: none listed. 2 contrasting citation statements in Scite tally (not reviewed).
sources.quality_note: Randomised comparison of ward models; 80 of 397 did not wear the monitor; numbers of upright events not given in the abstract.

sources.citation: Griffiths R, Babu S, Dixon P, Freeman N, Hurford D, Kelleher E, et al. Guideline for the management of hip fractures 2020: Guideline by the Association of Anaesthetists. Anaesthesia. 2021;76(2):225-237.

sources.population_setting: Peri-operative care of people with hip fracture, UK and Ireland
sources.tool_used: Google Drive read_file_content (open-access PDF, Drive file 1Sxil6oFaJOaKG9Vp9tmsITpj9ni_psjN); PubMed get_article_metadata
sources.quality_note: Used for its statement of the National Hip Fracture Database mobilisation indicator; PDF text is two-column and interleaved, passage reassembled from one column.

sources.citation: Zusman EZ, Dawes MG, Edwards N, Ashe MC. A systematic review of evidence for older adults' sedentary behavior and physical activity after hip fracture. Clin Rehabil. 2018;32(5):679-691.
sources.design: Systematic review of 14 studies (882 participants) measuring activity with monitors
sources.population_setting: Older adults with hip fracture in hospital, rehabilitation centres and the community
sources.quality_note: Small, heterogeneous studies; gives ranges, not pooled estimates.

sources.citation: Love AL, Cornwell PL, Whitehouse SL. Oropharyngeal dysphagia in an elderly post-operative hip fracture population: a prospective cohort study. Age Ageing. 2013;42(6):782-5.
sources.design: Prospective cohort
sources.population_setting: 181 patients (mean age 83, range 65-103) in a specialised orthogeriatric unit, Brisbane, Australia, assessed after hip fracture surgery
sources.quality_note: Single unit; assessment method and timing not given in abstract (authors are speech pathologists).

sources.citation: Suzuki M, Nagano A, Ueshima J, Saino Y, Kawase F, Kobayashi H, et al. Prevalence of dysphagia in patients after orthopedic surgery. Arch Gerontol Geriatr. 2024;119:105312.
sources.design: Scoping review with pooled prevalence (21 studies; 7 on hip fracture)
sources.population_setting: People aged 60 and over after orthopaedic surgery
sources.quality_note: Wide confidence interval for hip fracture (15% to 54%) reflects different methods and timing.

sources.citation: Mateos-Nozal J, Sanchez Garcia E, Romero Rodríguez E, Cruz-Jentoft AJ. Oropharyngeal dysphagia in older patients with hip fracture. Age Ageing. 2021;50(4):1416-1421.
sources.design: Prospective cohort
sources.population_setting: 320 patients (mean age 86.2) in an orthogeriatric unit, Madrid, Spain; Volume-Viscosity Swallow Test within 72 hours of surgery
sources.quality_note: Higher estimate than Love 2013, using a sensitive bedside test in an older group; shows how much prevalence depends on method.

sources.citation: Allen J, Greene M, Sabido I, Stretton M, Miles A. Economic costs of dysphagia among hospitalized patients. Laryngoscope. 2020;130(4):974-979.
sources.design: Retrospective parallel cohort using coded diagnoses
sources.population_setting: 2453 admissions with hip or femur fracture, Waitemata District Health Board, Auckland, New Zealand; 165 with a coded dysphagia diagnosis
sources.quality_note: Observational and unadjusted in the abstract; the dysphagia group was older (mean 85 vs 78) and coded dysphagia captures more obvious cases.

sources.citation: Baijens LW, Clavé P, Cras P, Ekberg O, Forster A, Kolb GF, et al. European Society for Swallowing Disorders - European Union Geriatric Medicine Society white paper: oropharyngeal dysphagia as a geriatric syndrome. Clin Interv Aging. 2016;11:1403-1428.
sources.design: Consensus position paper (two European specialist societies)
sources.population_setting: Older people with oropharyngeal dysphagia, all settings
sources.quality_note: Consensus document rather than a trial; used for warning signs and the upright-posture advice. Not hip-fracture specific. An RCSLT or NICE source for the signs was not found.

claims.claim: After a hip fracture, different abilities reach their best at different times: about 4 months for mood, arm function and thinking, and almost a year for leg function.
claims.supporting_passage: Community-residing hip fracture patients (n = 674) admitted to eight hospitals in Baltimore, Maryland, 1990-1991 were followed prospectively for 2 years from the time of hospitalization. ... Recuperation times were specific to area of function, ranging from approximately 4 months for depressive symptoms (3.9 months), upper extremity function (4.3 months), and cognition (4.4 months) to almost a year for lower extremity function (11.2 months).
claims.pico_timeframe: 674 community-dwelling adults with hip fracture, Baltimore 1990-91 / hip fracture and usual care / none / time to maximum recovery in 8 areas of function / 2 years
claims.safe_wording: In a large US study, leg function kept improving for close to a year after a hip fracture on average; mood, arm function and thinking reached their best at about 4 months.
claims.qualifications: Group averages from people who lived at home before the fracture, studied in 1990-91 in Baltimore. The time to reach a maximum is not the same as recovering fully; many never regain earlier function (see C03-12-b). Say 'on average' and 'one large US study'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Old cohort; care has changed. Dyer 2016 finds most recovery of walking and daily activities within 6 months, which is compatible (most gain early, some continues to about a year).

numbers.meaning: people followed, community-dwelling, Baltimore 1990-91
average time to maximum recovery for mood, arm function, thinking
average time to maximum recovery for leg function
range of new dependency in tasks (putting on trousers to climbing five stairs) among people independent in them before the fracture

claims.claim: Most recovery of walking and daily activities happens in the first 6 months, and only about half of people regain their previous mobility.
claims.supporting_passage: The bulk of recovery of walking ability and activities for daily living occurred within 6 months after fracture. Between 40 and 60 % of study participants recovered their pre-fracture level of mobility and ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living, while 40-70 % regained their level of independence for basic activities of daily living.
claims.pico_timeframe: Hip fracture cohorts (38 studies) / hip fracture / age-matched controls in some studies / mobility, ADL, accommodation / 3 months to several years
claims.safe_wording: Across many studies, most of the recovery in walking and daily activities came in the first 6 months, and roughly 4 to 6 in 10 people got back to the mobility they had before the fracture.
claims.qualifications: Ranges across studies of usual care, not predictions for one person. Fewer people from care homes recovered their earlier function.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Review authors note these figures show current outcomes, not what better rehabilitation could achieve.

numbers.meaning: period in which the bulk of recovery of walking and daily activities occurred
proportion recovering pre-fracture mobility and instrumental activities (range across studies)
proportion of hip fracture patients in Western countries moving into institutional care after fracture

claims.claim: Rehabilitation in hospital by a specialist multidisciplinary team probably means fewer people die or have to move to a care home in the following 6 to 12 months.
claims.supporting_passage: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation probably results in fewer cases of 'poor outcome' (death or deterioration in residential status, generally requiring institutional care) at 6 to 12 months' follow-up (risk ratio (RR) 0.88, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 0.98; 13 studies, 3036 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Based on an illustrative risk of 347 people with hip fracture with poor outcome in 1000 people followed up between 6 and 12 months, this equates to 41 (95% CI 7 to 69) fewer people with poor outcome after multidisciplinary rehabilitation.
claims.pico_timeframe: People 65 and over after hip fracture surgery / inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation supervised by a geriatrician or rehabilitation physician / usual care / death or deterioration in residential status / 6 to 12 months
claims.safe_wording: In trials, rehabilitation in hospital led by a specialist team probably meant fewer people died or needed a move to a care home over the next 6 to 12 months: about 31 in 100 compared with 35 in 100.
claims.qualifications: The outcome combines death and moving to a higher level of care; do not present it as care home moves alone. Moderate certainty. Trials of supported discharge and rehabilitation at home gave very low-certainty evidence, so do not claim that a 'supported trial at home' is proven to help.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Heterogeneous trials, most with unclear or high risk of bias for some items. Home-based supported discharge: very little confidence in findings of little or no difference.

numbers.meaning: illustrative risk of death or move to a higher level of care at 6 to 12 months with usual care
absolute reduction with inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation, i.e. about 31 in 100 vs 35 in 100
relative effect; 13 trials, 3036 people; moderate certainty

claims.claim: UK health policy in England and Scotland has advised against moving people into a care home directly from an acute hospital.
claims.supporting_passage: Both NHS England and the Scottish Government policy argue that care home admission from acute hospitals should be avoided
claims.location: Harrison 2017, full text, Background (secondary statement citing the policy documents); abstract: 'with policy documents advising against this transition'
claims.pico_timeframe: Policy statement as summarised in 2017; UK (England and Scotland)
claims.safe_wording: Policy in both England and Scotland has said that moving into a care home straight from an acute hospital ward should be avoided where possible.
claims.qualifications: Supported only through a 2017 peer-reviewed paper's summary of policy; the official documents themselves could not be opened, so do not quote their wording, do not say 'guidance says decisions must not be made in hospital', and do not name a specific document or year. The candidate's original wording ('decisions about long-term care are not normally made in an acute hospital') is not verified.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Current versions of the policies were not checked. Harrison 2017 is a single-centre Scottish study (mostly medical admissions) and has Alasdair MacLullich as a co-author, so it must not be presented as his own view.

claims.claim: (Optional context) In one Scottish hospital, just over half of decisions for a new care home move were made while the person was still on the acute hospital.
claims.supporting_passage: About 55% were in the acute hospital when the decision for a care home was made and 44% of that group were discharged directly from the acute hospital.
claims.location: Abstract, Results; full text, Discharge planning
claims.pico_timeframe: 100 people admitted from home and discharged to a care home, one Scottish teaching hospital, 2013-2015 / none / decision setting and timing
claims.safe_wording: In one Scottish hospital study of 100 people who moved into a care home after an emergency admission, just over half had the decision made while still on the acute hospital.
claims.qualifications: Not hip-fracture specific (most were medical admissions; 10% had fractures). Single centre. Alasdair MacLullich is a co-author. Optional; the post does not need it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Median decision time was 26 days after admission, not 'week two'; do not imply that decisions are typically made in week two.

numbers.meaning: of 100 people, in the acute hospital when the care home decision was made
median time from admission to the care home decision (range 0 to 249)

claims.claim: FRAIL-HIP studied 172 very frail care home residents aged 70 and over with limited life expectancy who broke a hip; after shared decision-making, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose an operation. It was not randomised.
claims.supporting_passage: Eligible patients were aged 70 years or older, frail, and institutionalized and sustained a femoral neck or pertrochanteric fracture. The term frail implied at least 1 of the following characteristics was present: malnutrition (body mass index ... <18.5) or cachexia, severe comorbidities (American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status class of IV or V), or severe mobility issues (Functional Ambulation Category ≤2). ... Of the 172 enrolled patients with proximal femoral fractures (median [25th and 75th percentile] age, 88 [85-92] years; 135 women [78%]), 88 opted for nonoperative management and 84 opted for operative management.
claims.location: Abstract, Design/Setting/Participants and Results; full-text excerpt: 'Only a randomized clinical trial would have avoided selection bias through the SDM process but was considered unfeasible and unethical.'
claims.pico_timeframe: Frail institutionalised adults 70+ with limited life expectancy and proximal femoral fracture, 25 Dutch hospitals, 2018-2020 / non-operative management chosen via shared decision-making / operative management / quality of life, mortality, satisfaction, quality of dying / 6 months
claims.safe_wording: A Dutch study followed 172 very frail care home residents (median age 88) who broke a hip and whose life expectancy was already short. After talking it through, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose an operation. People chose; they were not allocated at random.
claims.qualifications: Say near the top that it was a small, selected, non-randomised group who chose. Very frail and institutionalised; not applicable to most people with hip fracture.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the description.

numbers.meaning: participants, 25 Dutch hospitals
chose non-operative / operative management
median age

claims.claim: In the weeks after the fracture, quality of life (rated by relatives and carers) in people who chose no operation was not worse than in those who had an operation, within the study's preset margin.
claims.supporting_passage: The EQ-5D utility scores by proxies and caregivers in the nonoperative management group remained within the set 0.15 noninferiority limit of the operative management group (week 1 ... week 2 ... and week 4 ...). ... Although the short-term mortality in the nonoperative management group was higher than in the operative management group, there was no loss of QOL and HRQoL, and there was high treatment satisfaction and humane quality of dying.
claims.location: Abstract, Results; full-text excerpt (Discussion) via Scite
claims.pico_timeframe: As C03-22-a / proxy- and caregiver-rated EQ-5D at weeks 1, 2 and 4
claims.safe_wording: Relatives and care staff rated the person's quality of life in the following weeks as no worse, by the study's own test, when there was no operation.
claims.qualifications: Proxy-rated, not self-rated. Non-inferiority within a 0.15 margin, not 'the same'. Comparisons after about 30 days are unreliable because most of the non-operative group had died (authors' own limitation). Do not quote EQ-5D numbers (abstract confidence intervals look inconsistent).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors: 'given the even-higher-than-expected mortality rate in the nonoperative management group, the validity of the results comparing nonoperative management with operative management was reduced 30 days after the injury.'

numbers.meaning: pre-set non-inferiority margin on the EQ-5D utility scale (do not use in public posts)

claims.claim: Most people who chose no operation died within 30 days, but this reflects who chose it, not the effect of not operating.
claims.supporting_passage: The 30-day mortality rate was 83% (n = 73) in the nonoperative management group and 25% (n = 21) in the operative management group ... The high mortality rate was as expected given that we hypothesized that the frailest patients would opt for nonoperative management and that the explicit choice for nonoperative management would most likely result in an earlier palliative care approach compared with patients who opted for operative management.
claims.location: Abstract, Results; full-text excerpt (Discussion) via Scite. Also full text: 'Six months after the injury, 83 patients (94%) in the nonoperative management group and 40 patients (48%) in the operative management group had died'
claims.pico_timeframe: As C03-22-a / mortality at 30 days and 6 months
claims.safe_wording: About 8 in 10 of those who chose no operation died within a month, compared with 1 in 4 of those who had surgery. The frailest people, closest to death, were the ones who chose not to have surgery, so this gap does not show what the operation itself did.
claims.qualifications: Must not be read or presented as the effect of not operating. Even with surgery, about half had died by 6 months.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Selection by choice; no randomised evidence exists for this group.

numbers.meaning: 30-day mortality, non-operative group
30-day mortality, operative group
6-month mortality, non-operative vs operative

claims.claim: Relatives of about half of those who died without an operation rated the quality of dying as good to almost perfect.
claims.supporting_passage: The dying process in both groups was judged as humane (eTable 13 in Supplement 1). The quality of dying was rated as good-almost perfect by 26 proxies (51%) in the nonoperative management group, with only 2 proxies (4%) rating the process as terrible-poor. The quality of dying in the operative management group was scored as intermediate by most proxies (13 [62%]).
claims.location: Full-text excerpt (Results) via Scite; abstract gives the 26 (51%) figure
claims.pico_timeframe: Proxies of patients who died in the non-operative group / Quality of Dying and Death Questionnaire
claims.safe_wording: Among relatives who answered about a death without an operation, about half rated the dying as good to almost perfect; 2 rated it terrible or poor.
claims.qualifications: Denominator is proxies who completed the questionnaire (26 is 51%, so about 51 respondents), not all 88 people. Proxy judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Response rate not stated in the passages read.

numbers.meaning: proxies rating quality of dying good to almost perfect, non-operative group (of about 51 respondents)
proxies rating it terrible to poor

claims.claim: Care without an operation still needs active pain relief; in FRAIL-HIP the authors judged pain in the non-operative group to have been undertreated, and 2 people switched to surgery because of increasing pain.
claims.supporting_passage: The study results do suggest that pain in the nonoperative management group was undertreated and was a factor in end-of-life care that should be improved. ... After initially opting for nonoperative management, 2 patients were treated surgically within the index admission because of progressive pain.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C03-22-a / pain (PACSLAC) and analgesic use
claims.safe_wording: Even in this study, the researchers judged that pain was undertreated in the group without an operation, and 2 people changed to surgery because their pain grew worse. Care without an operation has to include good, regular pain relief.
claims.qualifications: This belongs in the post: it makes the 'care without an operation is active care' point honest.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Fewer people in the non-operative group had at least one adverse event (52% vs 81%), but adverse events were counted differently in people who died early.

numbers.meaning: people who switched from non-operative to operative care because of progressive pain
had at least one adverse event, non-operative vs operative (46 vs 68 people)

claims.claim: UK guidance treats surgery as the best pain relief for a broken hip and says surgery should still be considered even when the fracture comes with a terminal illness, as part of palliative care.
claims.supporting_passage: It is recognized surgery is the best form of analgesia and as over 30% present with cognitive impairment, it can be otherwise difficult to assess patients suffering. ... If a hip fracture complicates or precipitates a terminal illness, the multidisciplinary team should still consider the role of surgery, as part of a palliative care approach that: • minimises pain and other symptoms and • establishes patients' own priorities for rehabilitation and • considers patients' wishes about their end-of-life care.
claims.location: NICE CG124 full guideline 2011: Timing of surgery, guideline group discussion (page 65); Guideline summary recommendations (page 38)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with hip fracture, NHS England and Wales
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance (NICE) describes surgery as the best form of pain relief for a broken hip, and says that even when a hip fracture comes with a terminal illness, the team should still consider surgery as part of palliative care that eases pain and respects the person's wishes.
claims.qualifications: 'Best form of analgesia' is from the guideline group's discussion, not a numbered recommendation; attribute it as 'NICE's guideline group'. NICE does not set out when non-operative care is appropriate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: FRAIL-HIP authors note guidelines give no clear advice on non-operative treatment for frail people with limited life expectancy.

claims.claim: Scottish hip fracture standards allow for a decision not to operate, provided a management or palliative care plan is recorded and the decision is reviewed if the person improves.
claims.supporting_passage: Should conservative treatment be agreed, the management plan or palliative care plan, should be clearly recorded in the patient records. Best practice is to evaluate this decision should the patient's medical condition improve.
claims.pico_timeframe: Hip fracture care in Scotland
claims.safe_wording: Scotland's hip fracture standards expect that, if a decision not to operate is agreed, a clear care or palliative care plan is written down and the decision is looked at again if the person gets better.
claims.qualifications: Quote the standard only; do not state or imply Scottish Hip Fracture Audit results or Alasdair's role.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: In a gait study with pressure-sensing insoles, none of 16 people aged 75 and over after hip fracture surgery kept to a partial weight-bearing limit of 20 kg; 11 of 16 put more than twice that weight through the leg.
claims.supporting_passage: Both groups were instructed to maintain partial weight-bearing on the affected limb (≤20 kg) postoperatively. Following standardized physiotherapy training, gait analysis was performed. None of the patients in the elderly test group were able to comply with the weight-bearing restriction as recommended. We found that 69% (11 of 16) of the patients exceeded the specified load by more than twofold, whereas significantly more patients in the younger control group (>75% [14 of 18]) achieved almost the entire weight-bearing restriction (p < 0.001). Only 1 of the elderly patients was able to comply with the predetermined weight-bearing restriction, and only for a short period of time.
claims.pico_timeframe: 16 patients 75+ after hip fracture surgery vs 18 patients 18-40 after ankle fracture surgery / instruction to bear 20 kg or less after physiotherapy training / younger group / measured load during gait analysis / single session after surgery
claims.safe_wording: In a German study using pressure-sensing insoles, none of 16 older people after hip fracture surgery kept to a 'partial weight-bearing' limit when they walked (one managed it briefly); 11 of the 16 put more than twice the permitted weight through the leg. Most young adults with ankle fractures could keep to it.
claims.qualifications: Very small single-centre study, one walking session. Say 'none kept to it throughout; one managed briefly'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abstract gives the young group's compliance two ways (14 of 18 'almost the entire restriction'; 16 of 18 'maintained the partial load for nearly the entire time'); use '14 of 18' or say 'most'.

numbers.meaning: older hip fracture patients (aged 75+) tested
kept to the 20 kg limit as instructed (1 managed briefly)
exceeded the limit by more than twofold
prescribed partial weight-bearing limit
young ankle fracture patients who achieved almost the whole restriction

claims.claim: Told to partial weight-bear, older people after hip fracture walked less well and more slowly, yet put the same load through the leg as those allowed full weight-bearing.
claims.supporting_passage: The postoperative Parker Mobility Score in the PWB group compared to the FWB group was significantly reduced (3.21 vs. 4.73, p < 0.001). Accordingly, a significantly lower gait speed in the PWB group of 0.16 m/s vs. 0.28 m/s was seen (p = 0.003). No difference in weight bearing was observed in between the groups (average peak force 350.25 N vs. 353.08 N, p = 0.918), nor any differences in the demographic characteristics, ASA Score, Barthel Index or EQ5D.
claims.pico_timeframe: 41 older patients with pertrochanteric fracture, one German hospital / partial weight-bearing instruction (19) / full weight-bearing (22) / mobility score, gait speed, peak load / day 5 after surgery
claims.safe_wording: In a second small German study, older people told to limit weight on the leg after hip fracture surgery walked more slowly and had lower mobility scores on day 5 than those allowed full weight, but pressed just as hard through the leg.
claims.qualifications: Small, non-randomised (before-and-after groups), same research group as C03-19-a.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found that contradicts the mobility finding.

numbers.meaning: patients told partial vs full weight-bearing
gait speed on day 5, partial vs full weight-bearing
average peak force through the leg, no difference

claims.claim: NICE recommends that hip fracture surgery should aim to let the person bear full weight without restriction straight after the operation.
claims.supporting_passage: 4.2.6 Surgical procedures ➢ Operate on patients with the aim to allow them to fully weight bear (without restriction) in the immediate postoperative period.
claims.location: NICE CG124 full guideline 2011, Guideline summary, section 4.2.6 Surgical procedures
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults having hip fracture surgery, NHS England and Wales
claims.safe_wording: NICE guidance says surgeons should operate with the aim of letting the person put full weight on the leg, without restriction, straight after surgery.
claims.qualifications: Wording verified in the 2011 full guideline (not among the 2017 replaced recommendations); the current web version was not opened. BOAST wording not checked; do not cite BOAST.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Clinicians still restrict weight-bearing for some fractures and fixations (implant concerns); the guideline states an aim, not a ban.

claims.claim: Restricted weight-bearing after hip fracture surgery is linked with more complications and deaths.
claims.supporting_passage: Ottesen 2018: 'Controlling for patient and procedural factors, multivariate odds of any adverse event, major adverse event, delirium, infection, transfusion, length of stay ≥ 75th percentile (six days) and mortality within 30 days were all higher in patients with weight-bearing restrictions.' Tarrant 2022: 'In adjusted analysis, RWB did not influence 30-day mortality (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.15-01.13, p = 0.293) ... RWB was significantly related to increased DVT (OR 7.81, 95% CI: 1.81-33.71 p = 0.002) but no other secondary outcomes.' Xu 2026: 'Unrestricted weight-bearing was significantly associated with lower long-term mortality compared with restricted weight-bearing (RR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.51-0.88 ...). Short-term mortality did not differ significantly in the primary analysis ... No significant differences were observed for short-term complications, long-term complications, reoperation risk, or LOS between the two groups (all> 0.05). GRADE assessment showed low certainty of evidence for long-term mortality and short-term complications, and very low certainty of evidence for the remaining outcomes.'
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults after hip fracture surgery / restricted weight-bearing / weight-bearing as tolerated / complications, mortality, reoperation / 30 days to long term
claims.safe_wording: Studies disagree about harm. A large US database study linked restrictions with more complications and deaths within 30 days; an Australian study did not find more deaths; a 2026 review found restriction was linked with more deaths in the longer term, but the evidence was weak, and found no clear difference in complications or repeat operations.
claims.qualifications: Observational only: 'linked with', never 'causes'. Restriction is usually prescribed for harder fractures or fixations, so these links may reflect the injury, not the instruction. Do not give the Ottesen percentages (arithmetic inconsistency in abstract). Better to rest the post on the compliance and mobility findings plus NICE, and mention harm evidence as mixed.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Tarrant 2022 (only 58 restricted patients) found no mortality association; Xu 2026 low to very low certainty; the reassuring point for surgeons is that the review found no clear increase in reoperation with unrestricted weight-bearing (very low certainty).

numbers.meaning: patients over 60 in the 2016 US NSQIP hip fracture dataset (Ottesen)
patients with restricted weight-bearing in the Australian cohort (Tarrant)
2026 meta-analysis (Xu); low to very low certainty

claims.claim: In a Norwegian randomised trial, people on the fourth day after hip fracture surgery spent under an hour of the whole day upright (standing or walking): 58 minutes on average with comprehensive geriatric care and 45 minutes with orthopaedic ward care.
claims.supporting_passage: Primary outcome was measurement of upright time (standing and walking) recorded for 24 hours the fourth day postsurgery by a body-worn accelerometer-based activity monitor. ... A total of 317 (CGC n = 175, OC n = 142) participants wore the activity monitor for a 24-hour period. CGC participants had significantly more upright time (mean 57.6 vs 45.1 min, p = .016)
claims.pico_timeframe: 397 home-dwelling people 70+ with hip fracture who could walk 10 m before, Trondheim / comprehensive geriatric care on a geriatric ward with focus on mobilisation / orthopaedic ward care / upright minutes over 24 hours / day 4 after surgery
claims.safe_wording: In a Norwegian trial, people wore a small activity monitor for the whole of the fourth day after hip fracture surgery. On average they spent 58 minutes of the 24 hours standing or walking if cared for on a geriatric ward, and 45 minutes on an orthopaedic ward.
claims.qualifications: Averages on one day; people who lived at home and could walk before; 80 of 397 did not wear the monitor. The difference between wards comes from randomisation, so the geriatric care model can be said to increase upright time in this trial.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found against; consistent with the systematic review in C03-04-d.

numbers.meaning: mean upright minutes in 24 hours on day 4, comprehensive geriatric care (n=175)
mean upright minutes in 24 hours on day 4, orthopaedic care (n=142)
difference between arms (57.6 minus 45.1), p=0.016
minutes in 24 hours, for the comparison chart (derived)

claims.claim: Geriatric ward care also gave more separate times upright and better leg function on day 5, although the need for help to walk did not differ.
claims.supporting_passage: CGC participants had significantly more upright time (mean 57.6 vs 45.1 min, p = .016), higher number of upright events (p = .005) and better Short Physical Performance Battery scores (p = .002), than the OC participants. Cumulated Ambulation score did not differ between groups (p = .234).
claims.pico_timeframe: As C03-04-a / upright events (day 4), SPPB (day 5), Cumulated Ambulation Score (days 1-3)
claims.safe_wording: The geriatric ward group also got up more often during the day and had better leg function on day 5; the help they needed to walk in the first 3 days did not differ.
claims.qualifications: The number of upright events per day is not in the abstract; do not give a figure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: National hip fracture measures count whether mobilisation started by the day after surgery, and the Scottish standard counts getting out of bed to the toilet or into a chair as mobilisation.
claims.supporting_passage: Griffiths 2021: 'Based on National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance [20], the National Hip Fracture Database has adopted patient remobilisation on the day of or day after surgery as a Key Performance Indicator.' Scottish standards 2025: 'Standard 9a: Mobilisation is commenced by the end of the first day after surgery' ... 'ix Mobilisation can include getting out of bed to use the toilet or transferring onto a chair as well as more formal mobilisation with nursing or physiotherapy staff.' ... '9.4.1 The number of patients who had a surgical repair of their hip fracture who were mobilised by the end of the first day after surgery.'
claims.location: Griffiths 2021, Remobilisation section (two-column PDF text reassembled from one column); Scottish standards, Standard 9a, pages 27-28
claims.pico_timeframe: UK national hip fracture measures (NHFD KPI as described in 2020 guideline; Scottish standard v1.2, 2025)
claims.safe_wording: UK hip fracture measures record whether a person was got up by the day after surgery. Scotland's standard counts getting out of bed to the toilet or into a chair as a start. These measures record whether mobilisation started, not how long the person spends on their feet each day.
claims.qualifications: The final sentence is an accurate description of what the audit measure counts (a start of mobilisation by a deadline), based on the published definitions read; do not claim that wards 'rarely measure' upright time, which was not sourced. Do not state or imply Scottish Hip Fracture Audit results, and do not frame the post as Alasdair criticising the audit he chairs; NHFD indicator wording is as described in the 2020 guideline, current NHFD wording not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Scottish standard's rationale explicitly links early mobilisation with reducing deconditioning; the post should present upright time as a complementary measure, not a criticism of the standard.

numbers.value: by the end of the first day after surgery
numbers.meaning: Scottish Standard 9a deadline

numbers.value: day of or day after surgery
numbers.meaning: NHFD Key Performance Indicator (as described by Griffiths 2021)

claims.claim: Across studies using activity monitors, older people with hip fracture spend very little time upright in hospital (16 to 52 minutes a day) and remain inactive during recovery.
claims.supporting_passage: Older adults had excessive sedentary time (>10 hours/day) and low physical activity. Participants' average upright time differed across settings. During hospital stay, it ranged 16-52 minutes/day, while in the community, it ranged 51-261 minutes/day.
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with hip fracture in hospital, rehabilitation and community settings (14 studies, 882 people) / activity monitor measures
claims.safe_wording: Studies that fitted activity monitors found older people in hospital after a hip fracture spent on average between 16 and 52 minutes a day upright, and most of their waking day sitting or lying during recovery.
claims.qualifications: Ranges from small, varied studies. This replaces the candidate's uncertain 'Fleig 2016' claim on activity after discharge; community upright time ranged 51 to 261 minutes a day.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: range of average upright time in hospital across studies
range of average upright time in the community
sedentary time

claims.claim: In an Australian orthogeriatric unit, 34% of older people had swallowing difficulty after hip fracture surgery.
claims.supporting_passage: one hundred and eighty-one patients with a mean age of 83 years (range: 65-103) admitted to a specialised orthogeriatric unit were assessed for OD post-surgery for hip fracture. ... OD was found to be present post-operatively in 34% (n = 61) of the current population.
claims.pico_timeframe: 181 patients 65+ after hip fracture surgery, Brisbane orthogeriatric unit / postoperative swallowing assessment / prevalence
claims.safe_wording: In one Australian hospital unit, about 1 in 3 older people (61 of 181) had trouble swallowing after hip fracture surgery.
claims.qualifications: Single unit with formal assessment; name it as one study.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Estimates vary a lot with method and timing (see C03-07-b).

numbers.meaning: had oropharyngeal dysphagia after surgery
mean age (range 65 to 103)

claims.claim: Across studies, around a third of older people have swallowing problems after hip fracture surgery, with estimates ranging widely depending on how and when swallowing is tested.
claims.supporting_passage: Suzuki 2024: 'The estimated dysphagia prevalence rates [95 % confidence interval] of cervical spine disease, hip fractures, and others were 16 % [8-27], 32 % [15-54], and 6 % [4-8], respectively.' Mateos-Nozal 2021: 'a total of 320 patients (mean age 86.2 years, 73.4% women) were assessed for dysphagia within 72 hours post-surgery using the Volume-Viscosity Swallow Test. ... dysphagia was present in 176 (55%) patients.'
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults after hip fracture surgery / swallowing assessment within days of surgery / prevalence
claims.safe_wording: Studies that checked swallowing after hip fracture surgery found problems in roughly 1 in 3 older people on average, and more than half in one Spanish study that tested everyone with a bedside test.
claims.qualifications: Pooled estimate has wide uncertainty (15% to 54%). Say 'roughly a third' or 'between 1 in 3 and 1 in 2 in different studies'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A 2026 scoping review (not used as a source) reported extreme heterogeneity; some studies measured at discharge and found lower rates.

numbers.meaning: pooled prevalence after hip fracture surgery, 7 studies (scoping review)
prevalence in a Spanish orthogeriatric unit using a bedside test within 72 hours

claims.claim: Swallowing problems after hip fracture surgery were more likely in people who were older, lived in a care home, or already had neurological or lung conditions.
claims.supporting_passage: Multivariate logistic regression analyses revealed the presence of pre-existing neurological and respiratory medical co-morbidities, presence of post-operative delirium, age and living in a residential aged care facility prior to hospital admission to be associated with the post-operative OD.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C03-07-a / associated factors (multivariable)
claims.safe_wording: Trouble swallowing was more common in people who were older, came from a care home, or already had a neurological or lung condition.
claims.qualifications: Associations only. The study also lists postoperative delirium; the post can leave this out (delirium excluded as a topic) without misrepresenting the finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Mateos-Nozal 2021 identified dependence in daily activities before admission (and delirium) instead.

claims.claim: Swallowing problems after hip fracture are linked with aspiration pneumonia and higher death rates.
claims.supporting_passage: Two groups were identified and compared: those with a coded diagnosis of dysphagia (n = 165) in addition to hip/femur fracture (HF + D), and a group with hip fracture alone (HF-D) (n = 2,288) ... For those in the HF + D group, mean age was 85 years compared to 78 years in the HF-D group (P < .05) ... Mortality within 30 days of admission was significantly higher (18% vs. 4%,respectively) ... Rate of aspiration pneumonia was 14 times greater in HF + D (9.7%) compared with HF-D (0.7%).
claims.pico_timeframe: 2453 hip or femur fracture admissions, Auckland / coded dysphagia / no coded dysphagia / aspiration pneumonia, 30-day mortality / index admission and 30 days
claims.safe_wording: In a New Zealand hospital, people with hip fracture who had a recorded swallowing problem had aspiration pneumonia (chest infection from food or drink going the wrong way) far more often: about 1 in 10 compared with fewer than 1 in 100. They were also more likely to die within 30 days (18 in 100 vs 4 in 100). They were older, and this link does not show that the swallowing problem caused the deaths.
claims.qualifications: Observational, unadjusted in the abstract; the dysphagia group was 7 years older on average. Say 'linked with'. Do not say that watching the first drink prevents pneumonia; that has not been tested.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Boyapati 2024 (US, retrospective; not used as a source) reported a similar mortality association. No trial shows screening after hip fracture reduces pneumonia or death.

numbers.meaning: aspiration pneumonia, coded dysphagia (n=165) vs none (n=2288)
death within 30 days of admission, same groups (crude)
mean age of the two groups

claims.claim: Signs of a swallowing problem include coughing or choking on drinks, a change in the voice after swallowing, throat clearing, swallowing several times per mouthful and food left in the mouth; many older people do not notice their own swallowing problem.
claims.supporting_passage: Prominent among the main symptoms are aspiration, residue, excessive throat clearing, coughing, hoarse voice, atypical ventilation periods, and repetitive swallowing. An added risk is that many older people are unaware of their swallowing dysfunction. ... bedside clinical tests with water or other liquids together with oximetry, to look for coughing, choking, voice changes, and desaturation ... Clinical signs of impaired safety include cough, fall in oxygen saturation ≥3%, and voice changes; and signs of impaired efficacy include impaired labial seal, piecemeal deglutition, and oral and pharyngeal residue.
claims.location: Full text: 'Combination of symptoms' and 'Screening and clinical assessment of dysphagia' sections
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people with oropharyngeal dysphagia, any setting (consensus)
claims.safe_wording: Signs to watch for at a drink or meal: coughing or choking, a hoarse or changed voice after swallowing, lots of throat clearing, swallowing several times for one mouthful, or food left in the mouth. Many older people do not notice these problems themselves.
claims.qualifications: Source is a European consensus paper, not a UK (RCSLT or NICE) document; 'wet' or 'gurgly' voice is not the source's wording, use 'hoarse or changed voice'. 'Very slow eating' is not in the source; leave it out or use 'swallowing several times per mouthful'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Silent aspiration can occur without coughing; the absence of signs does not rule out a problem (the source notes many older people are unaware).

claims.pico_timeframe: Older people with oropharyngeal dysphagia (compensatory management advice)
claims.safe_wording: Sitting fully upright to eat and drink, and staying upright for about half an hour after a meal, is standard advice for people with swallowing difficulty.
claims.qualifications: Consensus advice for people with dysphagia, not trial evidence after hip fracture. Sitting upright after hip surgery may need help and good pain relief.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Ask the ward team whether swallowing has been checked, and ask for a swallowing assessment if you see these signs.
claims.qualifications: No opened source says which professions screen swallowing on UK orthopaedic wards; do not state that nurses (or any named staff group) can or should do it. Mateos-Nozal 2021 authors recommend 'Objective dysphagia assessment should be routinely included as part of the geriatric assessment of such patients' (usable if attributed).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not searched further to save usage.

candidates.reason: Recovery timing (Magaziner 2000; Dyer 2016) and the benefit of inpatient specialist rehabilitation (Cochrane 2021, moderate certainty) are supported. The UK policy claim is supported only as reported in Harrison 2017 (England and Scotland policy advises avoiding care home admission straight from an acute hospital); the candidate's exact wording 'not normally made in an acute hospital' is unverified and must not be used. The position (wait for rehabilitation before deciding a permanent move, where safe) is an ethical and practical judgement and should be marked as such. Supported discharge or a 'trial at home' has only very low-certainty evidence, so suggest it as an option to ask about, not as proven. Editor: owns the 'do not decide the care home move at the lowest point' argument; schedule away from C12-08.

FRAIL-HIP design, choices, proxy-rated quality of life, mortality and quality of dying are all confirmed from abstract and full-text excerpts; NICE full guideline supports 'surgery is the best form of analgesia' (guideline group discussion) and considering surgery even with terminal illness; Scottish standards require a recorded palliative plan when not operating. Mandatory qualifications: non-randomised, people chose; mortality gap reflects selection (authors say so); quality of life proxy-rated and non-inferior only within a margin; and the authors judged pain undertreated in the non-operative group, which the post must say (it supports the 'active care' point). Do not quote EQ-5D figures.

The inability of older people to keep to partial weight-bearing (Kammerlander 2018), reduced mobility without reduced load (Pfeufer 2019) and the NICE recommendation to aim for unrestricted full weight-bearing are supported. The candidate's core claim that restriction is 'linked with more complications' in a large US dataset is only partly supported: a 2022 Australian cohort found no mortality association and a 2026 meta-analysis rates the evidence low to very low certainty; the NSQIP abstract also has an arithmetic inconsistency. BOAST wording not checked.
candidates.revised_angle: Partial weight-bearing is an instruction most older people cannot follow: in small insole-sensor studies none of 16 people aged 75+ kept to it, and those told to restrict walked less and more slowly while loading the leg just as much. NICE says to operate so people can bear full weight straight away. Present harm evidence as mixed ('some studies link restriction with more complications; others do not'), not as a headline. Close with the question a physiotherapist can ask: what is the reason for the restriction, and how will this person move safely in the meantime?

candidates.reason: Reserve candidate. Taraldsen RCT upright minutes (57.6 vs 45.1 on day 4) and secondary outcomes confirmed from abstract; measure wording confirmed in the Association of Anaesthetists 2020 guideline (NHFD KPI: remobilisation on the day of or day after surgery) and the Scottish standards v1.2 (Standard 9a, with footnote counting getting out of bed to the toilet or a chair). Systematic review (Zusman 2018) confirms low upright time in hospital (16 to 52 min/day) and replaces the unsourced Fleig 2016 claim. Do not say wards 'rarely measure' upright time. Sensitivity: Alasdair chairs the Scottish Hip Fracture Audit, so present upright time as a complement to the standards, quote the standard's text only, and never imply audit results or his view of the audit. Judge: keep C03-23 from reusing the same trial; a practical ward measure (times out of bed per day) is not in the abstract, so any suggestion of it is a practice suggestion, not a finding.

Prevalence confirmed (Love 2013: 34%, 61 of 181; scoping review pooled 32% with wide uncertainty; up to 55% with systematic bedside testing). Link with aspiration pneumonia and 30-day death confirmed as an unadjusted observational association (Allen 2020). Warning signs and upright posture sourced to the ESSD-EUGMS consensus white paper (no RCSLT or NICE document found). Who can do a bedside screen on an orthopaedic ward was not found, so the post should ask families to request a swallowing check or assessment without naming a staff group. Do not claim that watching the first drink prevents pneumonia.
